draft.title: Art and culture under dictatorship
card: Dictatorships treated art, film, music and writing as tools of power. They wanted culture to spread the regime's ideas and to build loyalty to the leader and the state.

Artists, writers and filmmakers were pushed to make work that praised the regime. In the Soviet Union, this approach was called socialist realism. It showed workers, farmers and leaders as heroic and the future as bright.

Work seen as dangerous was banned. In Nazi Germany in 1933, books by Jewish authors and by writers who opposed the Nazis were burned. Modern art the Nazis disliked was labelled 'degenerate' and removed from galleries.
Those who refused to follow the rules could lose their jobs, be stopped from working, be jailed or leave the country. Many artists went into exile.
draft.remember: Dictators used culture to promote their ideas and banned work that challenged them.

a.q: Why did dictatorships such as Nazi Germany and Stalin's Soviet Union control art and writing so closely?
opts: They saw culture as a way to spread their ideas
They wanted artists to be free to sell abroad
They thought art had no effect on what people believed
They hoped to raise money by taxing galleries
a.why: Dictatorships saw art, film and writing as tools for shaping what people thought and for building loyalty to the regime. The claim that art had no effect is wrong, because the regime's close control shows they believed it mattered a great deal.
a.clue: Think about what the regime wanted people to believe.

b.q: In 1930s Moscow, a painter is asked to show a smiling crowd of farmers and a heroic leader. Which approach is the state asking for?
b.why: Socialist realism was the Soviet style that showed workers, farmers and leaders as heroic and the future as bright. Degenerate art is the Nazi label for modern work they banned, so it does not describe a request for praise.
b.clue: Which style praised the regime in a Soviet setting?

a.best: They saw culture as a way to spread their ideas
